item.title: Why Conformity Is Rational
item.description:
Conformity

Why Conformity Is Rational

"Fitting in" is a helpful strategy under the right conditions.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Asch and other researchers have shown humans sometimes conform even when it's completely irrational.
  • On the other hand, conformity can serve as a rational strategy to gain information in ambiguous situations.
  • We're always trying to balance many goals at once, like accuracy, social belonging, and personal authenticity.
  • Humans rely on shared knowledge, but conformity can become harmful when groups shut down dissenters.

In a classic moment of comedy history, the TV show "Candid Camera" had actors reveal the human tendency for conformity. In clips, you can see unsuspecting participants do things like enter an elevator and quickly conform to a new set of rules—like facing the back or turn from side to side—as they observe the actions of others.

Source: Candid Camera, ep. "Face the Rear" (1962)

This was inspired by a famous set of studies by social psychologist Solomon Asch at Swarthmore College in the 1950s. He conducted a series of experiments that seemed to expose a troubling side of human nature: a disturbing tendency to conform even when it makes no rational sense.

Asch invited groups of college students to complete a strikingly simple task. All they had to do was match the length of a line to one of three comparison lines. It was incredibly simple. You can try it yourself below: look at the line on the left and try to determine which line on the right is identical in length.

The answer is C. Or is it?
Source: Asch conformity experiments

Did you get it right? When students completed the task alone, they almost never made mistakes.

But Asch added a twist. In group settings, everyone except for one real participant was secretly in on the experiment. At key moments, these stooges deliberately chose obviously wrong answers—and the real participant, answering last, had to decide whether to trust their own eyes or go along with the crowd.

In this video, you can see the participant squirming uncomfortably as he is struggling with the decision to conform: does he trust his own lying eyes or those of his peers?

The results were startling: 76 percent of participants conformed at least once! And on average, people went along with the group about a third of the time.

It looked like a dramatic indictment of human irrationality. Crazy, right? But if we stop the story there, we might miss a far more interesting—and hopeful—truth.

Conformity Can Be Rational

Some conformity in Asch’s experiments was driven by what psychologists call normative influence: People wanted to fit in and avoid social discomfort. We know this because when participants could write down their answers anonymously, conformity rates plummeted. (BTW, this is a clever trick if you want to reduce conformity in groups—have them write down their opinions privately!)

So public pressure matters—yet not all conformity is about fitting in with the crowd. Much of the time, it’s a smart, rational response to uncertainty. There is extensive research in the past 70 years that has revealed the function of conformity.

In a series of studies Dom ran a few years ago, he gave participants harder visual tasks—ones where the answer wasn’t obvious.

Participants had to decide whether two shapes could be mentally rotated so that they matched. The key was that participants were under time pressure to respond, and for at least some of the trials, they were unsure of the correct answer.

Try it for yourself below:

Can the two shapes be rotated so that they match?
Source: Example of a Shepard-Metzler Task, Todd M. Gureckis

After a brief look at the shapes, participants saw a pie chart showing how (supposedly) previous participants had answered. We found that even when they were answering alone in private cubicles, participants shifted their answers toward the majority shown on the pie chart—whether or not that majority was correct.

This was a remarkably different pattern from Asch’s findings on conformity.

Because participants were alone, this wasn’t about social pressure. It was about using other people as a valuable source of information. Psychologists call this informational influence. When the world is ambiguous, trusting the crowd is often a rational thing to do. Perhaps they have useful knowledge.

Because it’s about the desire to get things right (rather than fit in), informational influence increases when people are motivated to be accurate.

Conformity Isn’t About Just One Goal

These findings expose an important truth: We’re always trying to balance multiple goals simultaneously, including:

  • Accuracy: Getting things right
  • Belonging: Fitting in and maintaining social harmony
  • Authenticity: Showing independence, signaling when we aren’t reliable sources, and maintaining a sense of personal integrity

Sometimes, you value peace over pedantry. If your friends insist on something stupid, you might sometimes suppress your better judgment for the sake of good vibes. Your broader truth is not about correcting every error; it’s about saying I am one of you.

For similar reasons, it’s uncomfortable to always go along with the group. Groups value people who bring new things to the table and are naturally suspicious of people who appear to have no opinions or standards of their own.

Conformity Is a Superpower and a Vulnerability

Humans’ ability to share information, coordinate, and align behavior is a profound strength. It’s what separates us from other species. No one person can master all the knowledge needed to navigate the world. We stand, as Newton said, on the shoulders of giants—and on the shoulders of one another.

But the very mechanisms that make conformity adaptive can, under certain conditions, lead us astray. When groups become insular, silence dissent, or grow overconfident in their collective narratives, informational and normative influence can tip into dysfunction.

Conformity, then, isn't irrational. Quite the opposite: Conformity reflects the deep rationality of social creatures trying to balance truth, trust, and identity.

The real challenge isn’t how to eliminate conformity. It’s how to build communities that prize good information, welcome dissent, and balance belonging with a commitment to truth.

In the right environments, conformity isn’t the enemy of reason—it's a part of how we reason as collective, community-oriented beings.

item.title: 5 Surprising Studies on Character Strengths
item.description:
Depression

5 Surprising Studies on Character Strengths

Important lessons for depression, leadership, and personal growth.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Depressed people can benefit from greater strengths use.
  • The underuse of character strengths is an important problem to address.
  • Character strengths are changeable, especially perspective, kindness, humor, hope, and gratitude.
  • Use a behavioral "nudge" to improve your character strengths use.
Source: AI-generated; Gemini/Google

I review about 100 character strengths studies per year. There are always a few studies that give me pause. I might see a counterintuitive finding, an idea I had not considered, or something that piques my signature strength of curiosity.

In this post, I share 5 surprising and interesting studies. These stopped me for a moment—literally—and I see immediate practical use from each.

These studies span many fields: workplace, coaching, clinical, and general audiences. I wonder if these studies give you an ah-ha, too!

1. Depressed People Can Improve Their Strengths

In this quasi-experimental study, 50 women with major depressive disorder were randomly assigned to eight positivity training sessions or a control condition. Positivity training significantly enhanced character strengths, improved time perspective (reducing past-negative and present-fatalistic while increasing past-positive, present-hedonistic, and future orientations), and increased self-awareness. This study shows character strengths are modifiable in clinical depression (Barzigar & Homaei, 2024).

Why is this striking? It is not typical for a positive psychology study to a) examine participants with an actual clinical disorder (it is, however, common in positive psychology studies to ask general questions about depression/anxiety); and b) it is novel to examine character strengths change amidst depression.

Practical strategy: If you’re helping someone with a clinical disorder like depression, bring character strengths into the assessment, the exploration of issues, and the treatment planning.

2. Spot Any Category of Character Strengths in Others

There are many lenses through which to view character strengths: signature strengths, lower character strengths, happiness strengths, achievement strengths, phasic strengths, and so on.

In a field experiment, 255 managers were randomly assigned to a strengths-spotting intervention focused either on employees’ signature strengths or on their lesser strengths. At the one-month follow-up, both interventions contributed positively to manager coaching behavior. This study showed that training in character strengths-spotting can be a useful tool for developing coaching behavior regardless of whether the focus is on signature strengths or lower strengths (Tobias et al., 2024).

Why is this striking? Strengths-spotting is often the first line of training/education that I offer students and other learners; therefore, strengths-spotting being a viable tool is not a surprise. What is interesting is the reminder that spotting any of an individual’s character strengths—whether high or low in their character strengths profile—can be beneficial.

Practical strategy: When you see a character strength in someone at work, call it out and explain the behavior connected to the strength.

3. Character Strengths Are Changeable, But There’s Far More We Don’t Know

A group of Spanish researchers wanted to know how changeable character strengths were and how common it was for the interventions to boost well-being. Their study examined 21 systematic reviews and synthesized 162 randomized-controlled studies (over 30,000 people).

Due to the strict, rigorous study-criteria, only 15 of the 24 character strengths could be examined from the lens of interventions. The results showed that 2/3 of the studies successfully increased the character strength being targeted and 63 percent improved well-being.

The character strengths with the strongest impact with interventions were kindness, humor, hope, perspective, and gratitude. Training in kindness (mainly self-compassion), love, and perspective (mainly mindfulness-based) produced the strongest gains in character strengths (Cebolla et al., 2025).

Why is this striking? The first-class scientific rigor was so strong that many character strengths (which have good, effective interventions) were excluded from the analysis. There is a callout here to the fields of psychology and positive psychology in that we need many more randomized-controlled studies to examine what is most effective. We cannot simply assume that something is effective because it seems to be.

Practical strategy: Consider one of the 24 character strengths you would like to improve. Chances are you can boost it, especially if you target one of the following: perspective, kindness, hope, humor, gratitude, love, self-regulation, spirituality, or forgiveness.

4. Love the Nudge

An interesting study (Deges et al., 2024) used semi-structured interviews to explore employees’ experiences of a signature strength, behavioral nudging intervention in the workplace. Nudges are low-cost environmental interventions that guide behavior and do not restrict choices we make. They often involve visual cues or creating new defaults and, in a workplace, aim to convert employees' mindful attention into emotion-driven behavioral change.

Three themes emerged in the study:

  • Nudges are key to converting strengths awareness into behavior change.
  • The active application of signature strengths depends on personal relevance.
  • Nudges can trigger a range of positive emotions.

Why is this striking? Labeling is powerful. Labeling interventions can create positive change. Practitioners of character strengths will respond here saying they “always” offer nudges to clients and students, they just never used that term. True, and having a label (i.e., nudge) and an emphasis (i.e., behavioral) and a framework (i.e., small nudges to enhance character strengths actions) can make all the difference.

Practical strategy: Set up positive nudges at work. For example, create a cue on your desktop to remind you to express gratitude (i.e., a screen-saver, an image, a video link). Cue your humility (i.e., sticky note that says “Listen first” as your desk). Program a mindfulness bell to sound intermittently on your computer—when it sounds, you pause, take two breaths, and ask yourself which character strength you might use in that moment.

5. Underusing Our Strengths is Worse Than Overusing Them

In one final study (on which I was a co-author), over 300 subjects took a new test, the Golden Mean Inventory—which measures the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of strengths—along with measures of depression, anxiety, psychotic symptoms, alcohol use, and suicidal behaviors. The results showed a general pattern of negative associations between character strengths and symptoms across problems. While an imbalance of strengths, as well as overuse and underuse patterns, predicted psychological problems, it was the underuse of character strengths that was a consistent indicator of symptoms (Parente et al., 2026).

Why is this striking? While strengths overuse is provocative and novel to many people, the underuse of strengths remains a central message in the science of character strengths. This means we can often use more of a strength in a situation or we could afford to manage the strength better (i.e., optimal use). While I’ve been arguing for 17 years that it is likely a bigger problem to underuse (in contrast to overuse) a strength, there is now strong data to support this.

Practical strategy: Identify the strengths you are vulnerable to underusing. Consider the context of your underuse—is it work, school, social, relational, or intrapersonal? Name one action you might take to explore or boost that underused strength in that context.

item.title: Finding Hope in the Face of a Child's Eating Disorder
item.description:
Eating Disorders

Finding Hope in the Face of a Child's Eating Disorder

Book review of "My Child Has an Eating Disorder."

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Eating disorders affect people of all body sizes, ages, and genders.
  • Parents often notice behavioural and emotional changes before physical signs appear.
  • Family support can play an important role in treatment and recovery.
  • Recovery is possible, though it rarely follows a straight or predictable path.
Source: Gül Işık / Pexels

When a child develops an eating disorder, parents are often left feeling frightened, confused, and overwhelmed. Questions quickly arise: What is happening? How serious is this? What should I do?

In My Child Has an Eating Disorder: An Essential Guide for Parents of Kids, Teens, and Adults, Alli Spotts-De Lazzer and Jenny Langley aim to answer these questions with a combination of clinical expertise, lived experience, and practical guidance. Drawing on their backgrounds in treatment and recovery support, the authors provide an accessible resource for families navigating one of the most challenging situations a parent can face.

While the book offers comprehensive information about eating disorders, its greatest strength lies in recognising that eating disorders affect entire families, not just the individual experiencing the illness.

Eating Disorders Are About More Than Food

One of the most important messages throughout the book is that eating disorders are complex psychiatric illnesses, rather than lifestyle choices or phases.

The authors explain a range of eating disorder presentations, including anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), and other specified feeding and eating disorders (OSFED). They also challenge common misconceptions, including the belief that eating disorders are simply about wanting to be thin.

Instead, the book presents eating disorders as conditions shaped by biological, psychological, social, and environmental factors. This broader perspective encourages families to move beyond blame and towards understanding.

Why Parents Often Feel Like They No Longer Recognise Their Child

One particularly powerful section addresses a concern many caregivers experience: feeling as though their child has changed completely.

The authors explain how eating disorders can influence behaviour, thinking, emotions, and relationships. Parents may see increased secrecy, irritability, withdrawal, or behaviours that seem entirely out of character. Several lived-experience contributors describe how the eating disorder voice often became stronger than their own intentions, leading them to say or do things they later regretted.

Understanding this distinction can help families respond with compassion while continuing to seek appropriate support.

Challenging the Stereotypes

The book repeatedly highlights that eating disorders do not fit a single image.

Many people still associate eating disorders with thin, adolescent girls. However, the authors emphasise that eating disorders affect people of different ages, genders, body sizes, and backgrounds. They discuss lesser-known presentations, including ARFID, as well as the possibility that one diagnosis may change into another over time.

This reminder is important because stereotypes can delay recognition and treatment. Some individuals may struggle for years before receiving appropriate support because their experiences do not match common assumptions.

The Importance of Supporting Parents Too

A theme running throughout the book is that recovery is not solely an individual process.

Parents and caregivers are encouraged to seek support, attend support groups, educate themselves about eating disorders, and examine their own beliefs about food, weight, and body image. The authors note that many people with eating disorders feel reassured when the adults around them are also doing their own work.

The book includes reflections from caregivers who describe feelings of guilt, fear, anger, isolation, and uncertainty. For many readers, these stories may be particularly validating. They reinforce an important message: needing support does not make someone a bad parent. Caring for a loved one with an eating disorder can be emotionally exhausting, and caregivers deserve support too.

Recovery Is Possible, Even When the Path Is Unclear

Perhaps the most hopeful aspect of the book is its discussion of recovery.

Rather than offering unrealistic promises, the authors acknowledge the uncertainty that often accompanies healing. Recovery timelines vary considerably, and there is no simple formula that guarantees success. Yet throughout the book there is a consistent emphasis on hope.

The authors describe recovery as more than the absence of symptoms. It involves developing a healthier relationship with food, exercise, and one's body, while building a meaningful and fulfilling life beyond the eating disorder.

For families who may feel discouraged by setbacks or slow progress, this message is both realistic and reassuring.

What Parents Can Take Away

Several practical lessons stand out from the book:

  • Trust your instincts if something feels wrong.
  • Learn about eating disorders from credible sources.
  • Focus on behaviours and well-being, not weight alone.
  • Seek support for yourself as well as your loved one.
  • Challenge common myths and stereotypes.
  • Remember that recovery is often non-linear.
  • Hold on to hope, even when progress feels slow.

Final Thoughts

My Child Has an Eating Disorder is more than a guide to diagnoses and treatment options. It is a compassionate resource that helps families understand the emotional realities of living alongside an eating disorder.

What makes the book particularly valuable is its balance of professional knowledge and lived experience. Rather than presenting recovery as a straightforward journey, it acknowledges uncertainty while offering practical guidance and genuine hope.

For parents, caregivers, and professionals alike, the book serves as a reminder that recovery is not simply about changing eating behaviours. It is also about rebuilding trust, strengthening relationships, and helping individuals reconnect with a life that feels meaningful beyond the eating disorder.
